leads.text:
Renaissance Midtown W. LLC v Lividini & Co., LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06265 
 October 27, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Renaissance Midtown West LLC, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 Lividini & Company, LLC, et al., Defendants-Respondents. 

 Decided and Entered: October 27, 2026 
 Index No. 659242/24|Appeal No. 7380|Case No. 2025-06285| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Kapnick, Shulman, Pitt-Burke, Hagler, JJ. 

 Berliner & Pilson, Great Neck (Richard J. Pilson of counsel), for appellant. 
 Tarter Krinsky & Drogin LLP, New York (David H. Wander of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lyle E. Frank, J.), entered July 24, 2025, which granted defendants' motion to dismiss the amended complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 The amended complaint was properly dismissed for lack of notice under paragraph 17(1) of the parties' lease. Paragraph 17(1) contains a conditional limitation permitting the landlord to terminate the lease for defaults other than nonpayment of rent— including "if the demised premises becomes vacant or deserted"— by serving a five-day notice to cure on the tenant "specifying the nature of said default." If the tenant fails to commence cure efforts within that period in good faith, "then Owner may serve a written three (3) days' notice of cancellation of th[e] lease upon Tenant," terminating the lease, and the tenant "shall remain liable as hereinafter provided." 
 The amended complaint specifically alleged that the tenant rendered the premises vacant while the lease remained in effect. This triggered the tenant's right to notice under paragraph 17(1) before plaintiff's reentry and reletting of the premises following the tenant's purportedly ineffective surrender ( see Holy Props. v Cole Prods. , 87 NY2d 130, 133-134 [1995]). 
 It does not avail plaintiff to argue that it was not intending to terminate the lease under this section but merely to collect unpaid rent owed for the balance of the lease term. The allegations that the tenant returned the keys without objection, following which plaintiff executed a new lease with a new tenant, are at odds with the continuation of the landlord-tenant relationship ( see e.g. Bay Plaza Estates v New York Univ. , 257 AD2d 472, 473 [1st Dept 1999]). In any event, both the lease and case law require notice to the tenant in advance of plaintiff's reentry and reletting of the premises ( see Holy Props. , 87 NY2d at 133-134 ). 
 Plaintiff's claims for unpaid amounts due under paragraphs 17(2) of the lease and 66 of the rider are also unavailing, as both provisions apply only when the tenant remains in possession of the premises. Paragraph 17(2) applies if "the notice provided for in [paragraph 17(1)] shall have been given, and the term shall expire as aforesaid; or if Tenant shall [be in] default in the payment of rent" or additional rent. The use of "or" excludes paragraph 17(2)'s application to circumstances to which paragraph 17(1) would apply ( see McKinney's Cons Laws of NY, Statutes § 235, Comment n 75). Because the amended complaint alleges that the tenant rendered the premises vacant, paragraph 17(1) applies here rather than paragraph 17(2). 
 [*2] 
 Paragraph 66 of the rider states, "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this lease it is agreed that any demand for rent may be made orally and no written notice of any kind shall be necessary as a condition precedent to commencement of a non-payment petition." This provision applies only where the tenant is in possession, as "a summary proceeding cannot be maintained against a tenant who is neither in possession nor claiming possession at the time of the commencement of the proceeding" ( Merrbill Holdings, LLC v Toscano , 59 Misc 3d 129[A] , *1-2, 2018 NY Slip Op 50410[U] [App Term, 2d Dept, 9th & 10th Jud Dists 2018]). 
 Accordingly, the claims in the amended complaint relying on allegations that the tenant's early vacatur in these circumstances did not constitute an effective surrender were properly dismissed under paragraph 17(1), as plaintiff was required to give notice to the tenant of its intention to reenter and relet the premises, which it acknowledges did not occur. Unlike in 622 Third Ave. Co. LLC v Hyatt Leader Ltd. ( 226 AD3d 463 [1st Dept 2024]), upon which plaintiff relies, the complaint contains no allegations that plaintiff responded to the tenant's notice of surrender of the premises by informing the tenant that the acceptance "was without prejudice to seeking damages for unpaid rent" ( id. at 464). Plaintiff acknowledges that there was no further communication between the parties after the tenant's counsel gave notice of its vacatur in August 2020 until plaintiff commenced this action in November 2024. 
 The court correctly dismissed the claims for breach of guaranty and for piercing the corporate veil against the tenant's principal. As the court properly determined, plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege the existence of a written and executed guaranty or to provide documentary evidence of the guaranty ( see General Obligations Law § 5-701[a] [2]). Although the lease submitted with the amended complaint contains a standard form guaranty, the form is blank and unexecuted. Plaintiff has not sufficiently alleged that a written and executed guaranty exists, nor has it asserted facts warranting leave to replead. 
 [*3] 
 With respect to the claim seeking to pierce the corporate veil, as an initial matter, the doctrine does not support a separately pleaded claim; "it is an assertion of facts and circumstances which will persuade the court to impose the corporate obligation on its owners" ( Cortlandt St. Recovery Corp. v Bonderman , 31 NY3d 30, 47 [2018]). To invoke the doctrine at the pleadings stage, plaintiff must allege that the tenant's principal "exercised complete domination and control over the corporation and abused the privilege of doing business in the corporate form to perpetrate a wrong or injustice" ( id. at 48 [internal quotation marks omitted]). The amended complaint asserts a bare allegation that the principal failed to maintain a separate bank account from the tenant in order to avoid damages. This allegation does not support plaintiff's contention that the principal dominated and controlled the corporation to perpetrate a wrong resulting in plaintiff's injury. 
 We have considered plaintiff's remaining contentions and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: October 27, 2026

OSCN Found Document:HUTZEL, ET AL. v. CITY OF NORMAN

 HUTZEL, ET AL. v. CITY OF NORMAN 2026 OK 77 Case Number: 124094 Decided: 10/27/2026 THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA 
 Cite as: 2026 OK 77, __ P.3d __ 

 NOTICE: THIS OPINION HAS NOT BEEN RELEASED FOR PUBLICATION. UNTIL RELEASED, IT IS SUBJECT TO REVISION OR WITHDRAWAL. 

 DIANNA LYNN HUTZEL, WILLIAM HARVEY COKER, and TERESA SUZANNE BORUM, Plaintiffs/Appellants, 

 vs. 

 CITY OF NORMAN, an Oklahoma municipal corporation, Defendant/Appellee. 

 ON APPEAL FROM THE DISTRICT COURT OF CLEVELAND COUNTY 

 Honorable Michael Tupper, District Judge 

 ¶0 Residents appeal from the dismissal of their petition claiming City violated the Oklahoma Constitution when it declared that a bond issue to fund a municipal homeless shelter passed by a majority vote. Residents also appeal the denial of a preliminary injunction barring City from issuing the bonds. This court retained the appeal. An exclusively city-owned "homeless shelter community facility" is a public utility as that term is used in Okla. Const. Art. 10, § 27. We affirm. 

 DISTRICT COURT'S JUDGMENT AFFIRMED. 

 Stephen Jones, William Jewell, Jones, Otjen & Jewell, Enid, Oklahoma, for Plaintiffs/Appellants. 

 Gregory M. Failing, GMF Legal Services, PLLC, Noble, Oklahoma, for Plaintiffs/Appellants. 

 Ryan Riddell, Ricky J. Knighton, II, Kathryn L. Walker, Norman, Oklahoma, for Defendant/Appellee. 

 Winchester, J : 

 ¶1 Today we consider whether a city-owned "homeless shelter community facility" is a public utility, as that term is used in Art. 10, § 27, of the Oklahoma Constitution, which allows cities to issue bonds to fund public utilities with the approval of a simple majority of voters. Defendant/Appellee the City of Norman (City) held an election to decide whether to issue tax-supported bonds to build a shelter and the proposition was approved by 54.25% of the votes cast. Plaintiffs/Appellants Diana Lynn Hutzel, William Harvey Coker, and Teresa Suzanne Borum (Residents) then sought a judgment declaring that the shelter was not a public utility and therefore required approval by a 60% super-majority to pass, pursuant to Art. 10, § 26, of the Oklahoma Constitution. City responded with a motion to dismiss, which the trial court granted following a hearing. 

 ¶2 Oklahoma authority does not support Residents' contention that only traditional infrastructure projects are public utilities under Section 27. Oklahoma cases have broadly interpreted "public utility" as used in Section 27 to include any city-owned property for public use or public benefit. On de novo review, we find the shelter is a public utility under Section 27 as a matter of law and City properly determined the proposition had passed with a simple majority vote. We therefore affirm the trial court's order dismissing Residents' petition. 

 FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 

 ¶3 The facts are undisputed. By Ordinance O-2526-36, the Norman City Council called an election to be held April 7, 2026, for approval or rejection of issuing $8,000,000 in general obligation bonds to fund a municipal homeless shelter. Paragraph (i) of the ordinance described the project: 

 Homeless Shelter Community Facilities: To provide funds for the purpose of acquiring, constructing, reconstructing, expanding, repairing, which may also include improving, renovating, acquiring and equipping a community facility to be exclusively owned by the City. 

 According to Section 1 of the ordinance, the question to be submitted to voters was: 

 PROPOSITION 5 

 Homeless Shelter Community Facility Bond Project 

 Shall the City of Norman, State of Oklahoma, incur an indebtedness by issuing its general obligation bonds in the sum of Eight Million Dollars ($8,000,000) to provide funds for the purpose of acquiring, constructing, reconstructing, expanding, repairing, which may also include improving, renovating, acquiring and equipping a community facility, to be owned exclusively by said City, to be completed with or without the use of other funds, and levy and collect an annual tax, in addition to all other taxes, upon all taxable property in said City sufficient to pay the interest on said bonds as it falls due, and also to constitute a sinking fund for the payment of the principal thereof when due, said bonds to be competitively sold and bear interest at the lowest rate not to exceed the rate of ten percentum (10%) per annum, payable semi-annually and to become due serially within twenty (20) years from their date? 

 The ordinance further provided: ". . . power is granted to City by Okla. Const. Art. 10, § 27 and law of the State of Oklahoma, to issue bonds to provide funds for such purposes, . . . ." The election results showed 54.25% of voters approved the bond issue. 

 ¶4 On April 14, 2026, Residents filed a Petition for Declaratory Judgment and Injunctive Relief. 

 ¶5 City responded with a motion to dismiss. City asserted that to be considered a public utility under Section 27, a facility must be publicly owned and advance the health, safety, or general welfare of the public. City cited cases finding a convention hall, 

 ¶6 Residents countered that this case presented a novel question of first impression, arguing Oklahoma courts had not extended application of Section 27 to a "welfare-conditioned social service facility," and that City's broad reading of Section 27 would effectively nullify Section 26. Residents also contended that City's acknowledgement that it could have sought approval for the bond under Okla. Const. Art. 10, § 35, presented another question of law preventing dismissal. 

 ¶7 City replied that the fact the bond could have been sought under Section 27 or Section 35 did not support Residents' claim that the bond required 60% approval under Section 26. City further noted that Barnes , supra , had included "almshouses" in its list of public utilities potentially embraced by Section 27. 

 ¶8 Following a hearing, held April 29, 2026, the trial court found the shelter was a public utility and therefore dismissed Residents' petition and denied their request for an injunction. Residents appeal. 

 STANDARD OF REVIEW 

 ¶9 It is settled that motions to dismiss are viewed with disfavor. May v. Mid-Century Ins. Co ., 2006 OK 100 151 P.3d 132 Id . Dismissal is appropriate only for lack of any cognizable legal theory to support the claim or for insufficient facts under a cognizable theory. Id . de novo. Lockhart v. Loosen , 1997 OK 103 943 P.2d 1074 de novo . Fanning v. Brown , 2004 OK 7 85 P.3d 841 Id . The essential question of law presented is whether a city-owned homeless shelter and community facility is a public utility subject to approval under Okla. Const. Art. 10, § 27. "(T)he question whether the use is a public use [under Section 27] is always ultimately a question for judicial determination; but, where the legislative judgment has been declared as to whether a given use is a public use, that judgment will not be overturned by the courts, unless it is clearly apparent that the same is without reasonable foundation." Barnes , supra , 1908 OK 191at 

 DISCUSSION 

 ¶10 Article 10 of the Oklahoma Constitution is devoted to public revenue and taxation; the sections at issue here address voter approval of indebtedness. Residents contend the bond issue was governed by Okla. Const. Art. 10, § 26, which bars any political subdivision from becoming indebted for any purpose, in amounts exceeding revenues but not exceeding 5% of the value of taxable property therein, without the approval of 60% of the votes cast. City contends the bond issue was governed by Okla. Const. Art. 10, § 27, as stated in the ordinance calling the election. That section allows cities or towns to become indebted in amounts greater than allowed by Section 26 to fund city-owned public utilities, upon the approval of a simple majority of voters. 

 ¶11 Section 27 is a self-executing "grant of power to the people of the municipalities of the state and not a limitation upon the Legislature." State v. Millar , 1908 OK 124 21 Okla. 448 96 P. 747 Shawnee , supra , 1959 OK 64at 

 The evident object and purpose of section 27, supra , is primarily to empower the incorporated cities and towns of this state by a majority of the qualified taxpaying voters voting at an election held for such purpose to become indebted in a larger amount than that specified in section 26, for the purpose of purchasing or constructing public utilities or for repairing the same, to be owned exclusively by such municipalities, and it is the duty of the court, if possible, to so construe the provision as to carry out its purpose. The construction of a constitutional provision must not be so strict or technical as to defeat the evident object and purpose of its adoption. 

 Millar, supra, 1908 OK 124at 

 ¶12 In their petition, Residents asserted the bond issue sought approval for indebtedness "for the construction of a city-owned permanent homeless shelter and resource center." Residents further alleged the shelter "is a public welfare and social-service facility providing housing, case management, and support services to a specific segment of the population experiencing homelessness. . . . It does not provide infrastructure services to the general public; it does not generate revenue through user fees in the manner of a utility; and it is not analogous to the categories of facilities Oklahoma courts have recognized under § 27." In its response to City's motion to dismiss, Residents averred "access is conditioned on a specific welfare criterion: the absence of stable housing. It is not open to the general public--it serves a defined subset of the population identified by circumstances beyond their control. This is a means-tested, status-based eligibility requirement of precisely the kind that distinguishes social-welfare facilities from public utilities." For purposes of this decision, we take these factual allegations as true. 

 ¶13 Residents contend "public utility" means universal infrastructure services, such as water, electricity, or gas, unconditionally available to the general public, Millar , supra , 1908 OK 124 

 There is a dearth of authority on what it takes to constitute a public utility. It is held in Valley City Salt Co. v. Brown , 7 W. Va. 191, that the expression "public utility" is synonymous with "public use." 

 In Aldridge v. Tuscumbia, C. & D. R. R. Co ., 2 Stew. & P. (Ala.) 199, 23 Am. Dec. 307, Mr. Chief Justice Lipscomb says: "Whatever is beneficially employed for the community is of public use." 

 In Olmstead v. Camp , 33 Conn. 532, 89 Am. Dec. 221, Mr. Justice McCurdy, speaking for the court, says: "One of the most common meanings of the word 'use,' as defined by Webster, is 'usefulness, utility, advantage, productive of benefit.' 'Public use' may therefore well mean public usefulness, utility, or advantage, or what is productive of general benefit." 

 Millar involved a bond issue to fund a sewer system, a project plainly within the "traditional infrastructure" meaning urged by Residents, and this court agreed it was a public utility. Id . at ¶ 38. However, the same year, in Barnes , supra , this court held that a project outside of traditional infrastructure was a public utility subject to Section 27. 

 ¶14 In Barnes , the plaintiffs opposed a bond issue to fund a convention hall on the ground that it was not a public utility. Recognizing that public utility meant public use, this court looked to definitions of public use that had emerged in eminent domain decisions. Barnes noted two views had emerged on what constitutes public use: "(o)ne is that a use to be a public use must be a use, or right of use, on the part of the public or some limited portion of it ; and the other is that it must be a public benefit utility, or advantage." 1908 OK 191at 

 ¶15 In considering whether a convention hall was a public use, the Barnes court cataloged various

FIFTH DIVISION
BROWN, C. J.,
MERCIER, P. J., and EPPS, J.
NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed. 
https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules
October 27, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A0908. HALL COUNTY et al. v. FAUL et al.
BROWN, Chief Judge.
Mark Douglas Faul and several other petitioners (collectively, “Petitioners”)
filed a petition in the trial court to challenge a rezoning decision, naming Hall County,
the Hall County Board of Commissioners, several Hall County employees, and several
individual property owners as respondents. Hall County and the Hall County Board
of Commissioners filed a motion for summary judgment arguing, in part, that the
claims were barred by sovereign immunity. The trial court denied the motion, and
Hall County and the Hall County Board of Commissioners appeal. For the following
reasons, we reverse the trial court’s denial of summary judgment. 
“On appeal from the denial or grant of summary judgment, the appellate court
conducts a de novo review of the evidence to determine whether there is a genuine
issue of material fact and whether the undisputed facts, viewed in the light most
favorable to the nonmoving party, warrant judgment as a matter of law.” Macon-Bibb
County v. Kalaski, 355 Ga. App. 24, 24 (842 SE2d 331) (2020) (punctuation omitted). 
So viewed, the record shows that in 2024, several property owners (“the
Property Owner Respondents”) submitted a rezoning application to Hall County,
seeking to rezone approximately 114 acres owned by the Property Owner Respondents
from “agricultural residential” zoning to a planned residential development. Faul,
who owns Arrowquest Services, Inc., that operates a winery on a 2.21-acre tract of
land in Hall County, opposed the rezoning. The Hall County Board of Commissioners
approved the application. 
Petitioners filed a petition pursuant to OCGA § 36-66-5.1(a)(1) in the Superior
Court of Hall County for review of the zoning decision. They named as respondents
Hall County, the Hall County Board of Commissioners, several Hall County
employees,1 and the Property Owner Respondents. Petitioners sought review of the
1 Petitioners named the Hall County Chairperson, members of the Hall County
Commission, and the Director of Planning and Zoning (the “Hall County
2
decision to rezone the approximately 114 acres for the purpose of the construction of
high density housing. Petitioners claimed they owned property that is adjacent to or
in the immediate vicinity of the rezoned property and asserted that they would suffer
“loss of business and business income, loss of property values, heavy and congested
traffic, ... substantial percentage decrease in the value of their properties[,] ... [and]
damages in the form of noise, odor, [and] mosquitos from excessive planned retention
ponds, water run-off and visual intrusions on peace and privacy.” In addition to their
appeal of the zoning decision, they brought claims for violation of due process, taking
without the payment of just and adequate compensation, and equal protection under
both the Georgia and United States Constitution. As relief, they requested to “have
the re-zoning reversed” and sought “both a temporary and permanent injunction as
well as a [d]eclaratory [j]udgment that the zoning decision appealed from is void.”
They also sought damages and attorney fees. 
 The respondents removed the case to the United States District Court for the
Northern District of Georgia pursuant to 28 USC §§ 1331, 1441, and 1446, but the
case was subsequently remanded after Petitioners dismissed their federal claims
employees”). 
3
pursuant to the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments of the United States Constitution
giving rise to federal question jurisdiction. 
 The Property Owner Respondents filed a motion for judgment on the pleadings
in the superior court, arguing, in part, that the entire action should be dismissed
because Petitioners failed to comply with the exclusivity provision of Ga. Const. of
1983, Art. I, Sec. II, Par. V(b)(2) (“Paragraph V”).2 Petitioners then moved to dismiss
the Hall County employees, but did not move to dismiss the Property Owner
Respondents or the Hall County Board of Commissioners, and filed a response in
opposition to the motion for judgment on the pleadings. The trial court granted the
motion to dismiss the Hall County employees. In a separate order, the trial court ruled
on the motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding, in part, that the voluntary
dismissal of the Hall County employees remedied any defect in the pleadings as it
related to the exclusivity provision of Paragraph V. 
Hall County and the Hall County Board of Commissioners filed a motion for
summary judgment. In the motion, they argued, in part, that sovereign immunity bars
2 As explained below, the exclusivity provision of Paragraph V requires that, in
order for there to be a waiver of sovereign immunity in actions seeking declaratory
relief, such actions must be brought “exclusively” against the State. See Ga. Const.
of 1983, Art. I, Sec. II, Par. V(b)(2). 
4
Petitioners’ claims because Petitioners failed to comply with the exclusivity provision
of Paragraph V, because although they had dismissed the individual county
employees, they failed to dismiss the Hall County Board of Commissioners. The
Property Owner Respondents also filed a motion for summary judgment. Petitioners
filed a response in opposition to both motions, in which they note that in addition to
their appeal of the zoning decision, they sought a declaratory judgment and damages
for inverse condemnation. 
The trial court denied the motions for summary judgment. As to the argument
regarding sovereign immunity, the trial court determined that the procedures
prescribed in OCGA § 36-66-5.1 and Paragraph V operated as a waiver of sovereign
immunity, and, therefore, the claims against Hall County, the Hall County Board of
Commissioners, and the Property Owner Respondents were allowed to proceed.3 Hall
County and the Hall County Board of Commissioners now appeal from the denial of
their motion for summary judgment. 
3 The trial court dismissed the claims of one petitioner based on lack of
standing. This dismissal is not at issue on appeal. 
5
1. Hall County and the Hall County Board of Commissioners argue that the trial
court erred by not dismissing the case because Petitioners failed to comply with the
exclusivity provision of Paragraph V. We agree.
“The doctrine of sovereign immunity, as enshrined in our Constitution, bars
suits against the State and its employees in their official capacities unless a statute or
the Constitution itself specifically waives that immunity.” State v. SASS Group, 315
Ga. 893, 893 (885 SE2d 761) (2023). In 2020, “an amendment to [Paragraph V(b)(1)]
of the Georgia Constitution that provides a waiver of sovereign immunity for actions
seeking declaratory relief from certain unlawful acts of the State or a local
government” was ratified. Warbler Invs., LLC v. City of Social Circle, 321 Ga. 125, 125
(913 SE2d 674) (2025). To the extent that citizens obtain a favorable ruling on their
claim for declaratory relief, they may then also seek injunctive relief to “enforce [the
court’s] judgment.” Ga. Const. of 1983 Art. I, Sec. II, Par. V(b)(1).4
4 Specifically, Ga. Const. of 1983, Art. I, Sec. II, Par.V(b)(1) states that 
[s]overeign immunity is hereby waived for actions in the superior court
seeking declaratory relief from acts of the state or any agency, authority,
branch, board, bureau, commission, department, office, or public
corporation of this state or officer or employee thereof or any county,
6
However, in order to take advantage of this new waiver of sovereign immunity,
the Georgia Constitution requires such actions to be brought “exclusively” against the
State. See Ga. Const. of 1983, Art. I, Sec. II, Par. V(b)(2). To comply with the
exclusivity provision of Paragraph V(b)(2), the plaintiff’s action
must be brought exclusively against the state and in the name of the State
of Georgia (or against the relevant local government as may be the case).
If a lawsuit does not comply, then the entire lawsuit must be dismissed[.]
SASS Group, 315 Ga. at 897(2) (punctuation omitted; emphasis added). See also Ga.
Const. of 1983, Art. I, Sec. II, Par. V(b)(2) (Actions filed pursuant to this Paragraph
against any county or county employee “shall be brought exclusively against such
county[,]” and “[a]ctions filed pursuant to this Paragraph naming as a defendant any
[entity] other than as expressly authorized under this Paragraph shall be dismissed.”). 
consolidated government, or municipality of this state or officer or
employee thereof outside the scope of lawful authority or in violation of
the laws or the Constitution of this state or the Constitution of the
United States. Sovereign immunity is further waived so that a court
awarding declaratory relief pursuant to this Paragraph may, only after
awarding declaratory relief, enjoin such acts to enforce its judgment.
7
The Supreme Court of Georgia has held that when a plaintiff tries to avail
themselves “of Paragraph V’s waiver of sovereign immunity in any way—i.e., even
for one claim—then it is an action filed pursuant to Paragraph V.” Lovell v.
Raffensperger, 318 Ga. 48, 50(2)(a) (897 SE2d 440) (2024), citing SASS Group, 315
Ga. at 897(2) (finding that pro se plaintiffs relied, at least partially, on Paragraph V’s
waiver of sovereign immunity where they sought a declaratory judgment and
injunctive relief against the State of Georgia and thus, the lawsuit that also named a
state actor as a defendant should be dismissed). If a lawsuit does not comply with this
exclusivity requirement, “then the entire lawsuit must be dismissed, even if some
claims within the lawsuit could have otherwise been brought on their own without
relying on Paragraph V’s waiver.” Lovell, 318 Ga. at 50(2)(a). But see Garner v.
Clayton County, 378 Ga. App. 618, 624–25(3) (926 SE2d 842) (2026) (holding that the
trial court erred by dismissing a complaint seeking declaratory and injunctive relief
where the plaintiff explicitly provided she was not relying on Paragraph V’s waiver of
sovereign immunity but instead was relying on a waiver of sovereign immunity in
Georgia’s Open Records Act, OCGA § 50-18-70 et seq.).
8
Here, Petitioners filed their action against Hall County, the Hall County Board
of Commissioners, the Hall County employees, and the Property Owner Respondents.
Their petition included a claim for a declaratory judgment that the rezoning decision
was void. Although Petitioners dismissed the Hall County employees, the claims
against the Hall County Board of Commissioners and the Property Owner
Respondents were still pending at the time the trial court denied the motion for
summary judgment. Because Petitioners were relying, at least partially, on Paragraph
V’s waiver of sovereign immunity by seeking a declaratory judgment, the suit was due
to be dismissed in its entirety on the basis that it also named as defendants the Hall
County Board of Commissioners and the Property Owner Respondents. First Ctr., Inc.
v. Cobb County, 318 Ga. 271, 272 (897 SE2d 854) (2024) (affirming dismissal of action
for failing to comply with Paragraph V’s exclusivity provision where the appellants
brought an action setting forth numerous counts, including claims for declaratory,
injunctive, and mandamus relief, against the county, the county commissioner, and
the zoning division manager). 
Petitioners argue that dismissal is not required because the naming of additional
parties is merely a procedural defect that may be cured, rather than a jurisdictional
9
defect, citing Warbler, 321 Ga. at 125. In Warbler, our Supreme Court held that a
failure to comply with the exclusivity provision of Paragraph V “is not a jurisdictional
bar to hearing the case,” and was merely a procedural “naming requiremen

leads.caseName: Dominique AC Reed v. Carl Lee Hill
leads.text:
TEXAS COURT OF APPEALS, THIRD DISTRICT, AT AUSTIN

 NO. 03-26-00362-CV

 Dominique AC Reed, Appellant

 v.

 Carl Lee Hill, Appellee

 FROM THE 146TH DISTRICT COURT OF BELL COUNTY
 NO. 23DFAM337543, THE HONORABLE MIKE RUSSELL, JUDGE PRESIDING

 MEMORANDUM OPINION

 Appellant Dominique AC Reed filed a notice of appeal challenging the trial

court’s “Order to Release Funds to Petitioner,” which ordered the release of $10,493.33, together

with 90% of the accrued interest, from the trial court’s registry to appellee Carl Lee Hill, and

which also denied Reed’s emergency motion. Upon initial review, the Clerk of this Court sent

Reed a letter informing her that this Court appears to lack jurisdiction over the appeal because

the January 6, 2026 “Order to Release Funds to Petitioner” in the clerk’s record does not appear

to be a final and appealable judgment, and our jurisdiction is limited to appeals in which there

exists a final or appealable judgment or order. See Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 51.012;

Lehmann v. Har-Con Corp., 39 S.W.3d 191, 195 (Tex. 2001) (explaining that appeal generally

may only be taken from final judgment that disposes of all pending parties and claims in record

unless statute provides for interlocutory appeal).
  The Clerk further informed Reed that once the trial court loses plenary power

after a final judgment such as the 2024 divorce decree, or a mandate from any appeal issues, “the

trial court does not have the authority to make a new order that is inconsistent with the original

judgment.” Beeler v. Fuqua, No. 09-07-358CV, 2007 WL 2962799, at *1 (Tex. App.—

Beaumont Oct. 11, 2007, pet. denied) (mem. op.). In this case, the trial court’s order to pay the

funds in the court’s registry appears to be “nothing more than the satisfaction of the trial court’s

ministerial duty to give effect to the mandate.” Id. Because “[n]o appeal lies from a

post-judgment order that is within the trial court’s enforcement powers, not inconsistent with the

original judgment, and does not materially change the substantive portions of the judgment,” it

appears that the trial court’s order is not an appealable order. Id.

 The Clerk requested a response from Reed explaining any basis that exists for this

Court’s jurisdiction. Reed filed a response. 1 In her response, she contends that the trial court’s

January 6, 2026 order is reviewable on appeal because “[i]t was the first order resolving the

parties’ competing claims to actual funds that became available in the trial court’s registry after

sale of the marital residence.” She further asserts that the trial court “had expressly reserved

reimbursement, expenses, attorney’s fees, and distribution of funds for a later proceeding when

money reached the registry.” Reed relies on Alexander Dubose Jefferson & Townsend LLP

v. Chevron Phillips Chem. Co., L.P., 540 S.W.3d 577, 587-88 (Tex. 2018), asserting that the trial

court’s release order here is comparable to the order in Alexander Dubose that the Texas

 1 The Court twice extended Reed’s deadline to file her response. Her response was filed
two days after the extended deadline, but Reed moved for leave to file her response out of time
under cover of her response. The Court grants Reed’s motion for leave to file her response out
of time.

 2
 Supreme Court determined was final and appealable because it “was the first determination of

competing substantive ownership rights” to the funds pending in the court’s registry. Id. at 588.

 We disagree. In Alexander Dubose, the issue before the court was whether

Alexander Dubose’s failure to timely appeal a turnover order deprived the court of appeals of

jurisdiction. Id. at 578. The court held that “a turnover order is not a final, appealable judgment

when it merely orders funds subject to an as-yet-unadjudicated ownership dispute into the court's

registry.” Id. The lawsuit that led to the post-judgment turnover proceeding to enforce a final

monetary judgment was a complex suit involving multiple claims and parties. Id. The turnover

order at issue stated that it was without prejudice to the right of two of the parties to seek the

release of the funds “to be held initially in the Court’s Registry” and it was silent as to one

party’s intervention and request for a declaration and the other party’s motion to strike. Id. at

579. The latter party later filed a motion for final judgment on the other party’s intervention and

a motion to enforce the turnover order and have the funds released to it because the intervening

party had not appealed the turnover order. Id. at 580. The trial court subsequently signed a

release order denying the intervening party’s motion to release the registry funds, ordering the

turnover order enforced and funds released to the other party, and declaring that the order is a

final judgment and “as such is appealable.” Id. On appeal from that order, the court of appeals

dismissed the appeal for want of jurisdiction, holding that the intervening party should have

appealed the turnover order, not the release order, because the turnover order was the final,

appealable judgment. Id.

 In analyzing the finality issue, the Texas Supreme Court explained that a trial

court’s post-judgment enforcement power, in contrast with plenary power, is of uncertain

duration because it lasts until the judgment is satisfied. Id. at 581. Accordingly, “the finality of

 3
 enforcement orders, including turnover orders, can become uncertain,” id., and “what qualifies as

‘final’ in the turnover context necessarily diverges from the more traditional concept of finality,”

id. at 582. The court analyzed whether the trial court had ever ruled upon the merits of the

intervening party’s claims to the disputed funds before it analyzed the finality of the turnover

order. See id. at 582-86. It concluded that the trial court had not decided the party’s substantive

claims to the disputed funds until the issuance of the release order. Id. at 586.

 The court then analyzed whether the provision of the turnover order directing

funds into the registry could function as a mandatory injunction, and thus a final, appealable

judgment when the trial court had never determined the intervening party’s substantive

ownership rights to the funds. Id. The court determined that the intervening party’s motion to

release the funds, which “simultaneously requested a final conclusion as to its pending,

competing claims and an order conclusively establishing entitlement to the funds pending in the

court’s registry,” sought relief that the trial court had not yet ruled upon. Id. at 588. Because the

release order “was the first order that spoke to the merits of [the intervening party’s] pending and

competing ownership claim,” the court concluded that it was more than an order merely

affirming the turnover order. Id. Instead, the court held that the release order “was the first

determination of competing substantive ownership rights and was the final, appealable

judgment.” Id.

 In contrast, here, the divorce decree (which Reed did not appeal) determined the

merits of the parties’ substantive ownership rights to the funds. The decree established that the

property at issue was to be sold, “under terms and conditions determined by a court-appointed

receiver” with the party at fault for the necessity of appointing a receiver to be ordered “to pay

all fees associated with the appointment of the receiver, including attorney’s fees and court

 4
 costs” with the money to be taken from the proceeds from the sale of the home. Reed was

awarded the exclusive right to the use and possession of the home until December 6, 2023, but

was ordered to move out on or before six months after December 6, 2023. Hill was ordered to

make the payments of principal, interest, taxes, and insurance on the property during the

pendency of the sale, and “[a]ll reasonable repairs necessary to keep the property in its present

condition.” The decree stated,

 The net sales proceeds (defined as the gross sales price less cost of sale and full
 payment of any mortgage indebtedness or liens on the property) shall be
 distributed as follows:

 1. Carl Hill shall be reimbursed for one-half of each month the mortgage is paid
 after December 6, 2023.

 2. Carl Hill shall be reimbursed for any reasonable repairs made to the home
 prior to the sale of the home.

 3. Any reimbursement, if necessary, in accordance with an appraisal or costs
 associated with the appointment of a receiver in accordance with any further
 Order of this Court, as necessary.

 4. The remaining proceeds shall be split equally between the parties.

Hill filed a petition for enforcement of the property division in September 2024, alleging that

Reed refused to vacate the property and was not cooperating in the sale of the property. Hill also

moved for the appointment of a receiver. After an evidentiary hearing, the trial court determined

that “proper grounds exist for the appointment of a receiver.” Reed did not appeal the order

appointing the receiver. In August 2025, the trial court signed an order approving the sale of

the property.

 In October and November 2025, Reed filed an emergency motion for partial

distribution of funds from receivership estate, a supplemental motion for partial withdrawal of

 5
 funds from court registry (supplementing her October motion), and a notice of adverse appellate

ruling and renewed request for emergency motion. None of these motions assert that Reed has a

superior right to have the proceeds in the court’s registry awarded to her before Hill is

reimbursed as the decree requires. Instead, Reed’s arguments focus on her need for the funds

and her argument that Hill engaged in unspecified “material misrepresentations and conduct

amounting to unclean hands, which directly contributed to the wrongful dimunition of [Reed’s]

awarded equity.” According to Hill, the trial court held a telephonic hearing on these motions on

November 25, 2025, and denied Reed’s request for relief.

 In December 2025, Hill filed a motion to withdraw funds and response to Reed’s

emergency motion. At the hearing, the trial court did not hear evidence related to the merits of

the parties’ “competing substantive ownership rights” to the funds in the registry. See id. The

merits of those ownership rights to the funds had been determined in the decree. The only

evidence that the trial court received was evidence that the receiver deposited the proceeds of the

sale of the property, which amounted to $10,493.33, in the trial court’s registry and that Hill paid

$56,092.18 in mortgage payments between December 2023 and August 2025 (when the court

approved the receiver’s sale of the property), half of which is $28,046.09. The trial court also

took judicial notice of its file, and Hill submitted the divorce decree as an exhibit.

 The trial court’s order releasing the funds to Hill is “a post-judgment order that is

within the trial court’s enforcement powers, not inconsistent with the original judgment, and

does not materially change the substantive portions of the judgment.” Beeler, 2007 WL

2962799, at *1. No appeal lies from such an order. Id.

 Accordingly, for the reasons explained above, we dismiss the appeal for want of

jurisdiction. See Tex. R. App. P. 42.3(a).

 6
  __________________________________________
 Gisela D. Triana, Justice

Before Justices Triana, Crump, and Ellis

Dismissed for Want of Jurisdiction

Filed: October 27, 2026

  Citibank, N.A. v. Burke

 CITIBANK, N.A., TRUSTEE v. HILDA
 MARIE BURKE ET AL.
 (AC 48516)
 Suarez, Seeley and Westbrook, Js.

 Syllabus

The defendants, S and H, appealed, and the substitute plaintiff cross appealed,
from the trial court’s judgment finding, inter alia, that, although the substi-
tute plaintiff had established a prima facie case of foreclosure with respect
to a mortgage on certain of H’s real property that secured a note executed
by S, the defendants had proven, by a preponderance of the evidence, their
first special defense and count one of their counterclaim, alleging improper
default on the loan and wrongful foreclosure. The defendants claimed, inter
alia, that the court erred in ordering them to pay the substitute plaintiff a
certain sum to bring the loan current. The substitute plaintiff claimed, inter
alia, that the court erred in finding that S timely reinstated the loan. Held:

The trial court’s findings that a mortgage statement issued by the substitute
plaintiff’s loan servicer to the defendants constituted an offer to bring the
loan current and thereby reinstate the loan and that S’s payment in accordance
with that statement served as the consideration to reinstate the loan were
clearly erroneous, as it was not reasonable for S to conclude that sending a
payment in accordance with the mortgage statement would bring the loan
current, given that S had been informed multiple times that the amount
listed in the mortgage statement was not sufficient to reinstate the loan, the
alleged agreement to reinstate the loan lacked consideration, as there was
no evidence before the court of a promise by the defendants to do something
that they were not already required to do, and S had failed to meet the condi-
tions under the mortgage for reinstatement of the loan after acceleration.

This court lacked authority to order the trial court to render a judgment of
foreclosure and, accordingly, remanded the case for further proceedings to
determine the form of foreclosure judgment, if any, to be rendered and the
amount of the debt, as, although this court determined that the substitute
plaintiff had established a prima facie case of foreclosure, the determination
of what equity required was a matter for the trial court.

 Argued May 18—officially released October 27, 2026

 Procedural History

 Action to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property
of the named defendant, and for other relief, brought to
the Superior Court in the judicial district of Fairfield,
where U.S. Bank Trust, National Association, Not in
its Individual Capacity but solely as Owner Trustee for
VRMTG Asset Trust, was substituted as the plaintiff;
  Citibank, N.A. v. Burke

thereafter, the named defendant et al. filed a counter-
claim; subsequently, the case was tried to the court,
Cirello, J.; judgment in part for the plaintiff and in part
for the named defendant et al. on the counterclaim, from
which the named defendant et al. appealed and the sub-
stitute plaintiff cross appealed to this court. Reversed;
further proceedings.
 Bruce L. Elstein, with whom, on the brief, was John J.
Ribas, for the appellants-cross appellees (named defen-
dant et al.).
 Crystal L. Cooke, with whom, on the brief, was Tara
L. Trifon, for the appellee-cross appellant (substitute
plaintiff).

 Opinion

 SEELEY, J. The defendants Hilda Marie Burke (Hilda)
and Stephen P. Burke (Stephen) appeal,1 and the substi-
tute plaintiff, U.S. Bank Trust, National Association,
Not in its Individual Capacity but solely as Owner Trustee
for VRMTG Asset Trust (U.S. Bank), cross appeals, from
the judgment of the trial court rendered in this action
to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property owned
by Hilda, which secured a promissory note that had been
executed by Stephen, who defaulted on the note. On
appeal, the defendants claim that the court erred in (1)
ordering them to pay U.S. Bank $355,913.20, despite
having found in their favor with respect to their first spe-
cial defense and count one of their counterclaim, which
alleged that U.S. Bank was not entitled to foreclosure due
to improper default on the note, (2) not tolling any inter-
est claimed by U.S. Bank, and (3) not ordering U.S. Bank
to correct negative credit reports pertaining to Stephen,
given the court’s finding that the defaulted loan had
been successfully reinstated. On cross appeal, U.S. Bank
 1
 Other defendants in this action include the Department of Revenue
Services for the state of Connecticut and Bank of America, N.A. Those
defendants are not involved in this appeal. Accordingly, we refer to
Hilda and Stephen individually by name when necessary and collectively
as the defendants.
  Citibank, N.A. v. Burke

claims that the court erred in finding that (1) a monthly
mortgage statement dated May 11, 2019, that was sent
to Stephen (May mortgage statement) constituted an
offer to reinstate the loan after the promissory note was
accelerated due to Stephen’s default, (2) Stephen entered
into a contract with U.S. Bank and/or its loan servicer to
reinstate the loan by sending a payment of $39,861.97,
which was received on June 13, 2019, (3) Stephen timely
reinstated the loan, (4) U.S. Bank wrongfully rejected
the $39,861.97 payment, (5) U.S. Bank was prohibited
from foreclosing on the basis of equitable considerations,
and (6) the defendants proved, by a preponderance of
the evidence, their first special defense and count one
of their counterclaim, alleging improper default on the
loan and wrongful foreclosure. With respect to the cross

In light of that determination, which is dispositive of
most of the other claims raised in the cross appeal and
all of the claims raised in the defendants’ direct appeal,
we reverse the judgment of the court.
 The following facts, to which the parties stipulated,

shall be reformed to state: ‘(D) Note means the promissory note signed
by [Stephen] and dated July 11, 2005. The note states that [Stephen]
owed the lender nine hundred seventy-five thousand & 00/100 dollars

Filed 10/23/26 Seligman Liberty Station v. City of San Diego CA3 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED 
California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions not certified for 
publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has not been certified for publication 
or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
THIRD APPELLATE DISTRICT 
(Sacramento) 
SELIGMAN LIBERTY STATION, LLC et al., 
 Plaintiffs and Appellants, 

 v. 

CITY OF SAN DIEGO et al., 
 Defendants and Respondents. 
C101420 

(Super. Ct. No. 34-2022-
80003837-CU-WM-GDS) 

Plaintiffs and appellants Seligman Liberty Station, LLC, et al. (collectively 
referred to as the plural Seligman), petitioned for a writ of mandate requiring respondent 
City of San Diego (City) to sell certain specified properties the City had retained as 
“future development” properties following the dissolution of California’s redevelopment 
agencies. (See Assem. Bill No. 26 (2011-2012 1st Ex. Sess.) enacted by Stats. 2011, 1st 
Ex. Sess. 2011-2012, chs. 5-6 (Assembly Bill No. 1X 26); see also Assem. Bill No. 1484 
(2011-2012 Reg. Sess.) enacted by Stats. 2012, ch. 26, §§ 6-35 (Assembly No. Bill 
1484).)
1 The trial court granted Seligman’s petition for writ of mandate in part and 
issued a peremptory writ of mandate directing the City to take certain actions with respect 
to the retained subject properties. 

1 We refer to the cumulative operation of Assembly Bill No. 1x 26 and Assembly 
Bill No. 1484 as the Dissolution Law. 
2 
Seligman filed a postjudgment motion for attorney fees. The trial court found that 
Seligman were entitled to attorney fees under Code of Civil Procedure section 1021.5,2 
but it awarded fees in an amount substantially less than the amount Seligman sought. In 
this appeal from the order awarding attorney fees, Seligman contend the court abused its 
discretion when it awarded fees in a reduced amount. No abuse of discretion appears, 
and therefore we will affirm the order. 
BACKGROUND 
Dissolution Law 
The California Supreme Court has explained the history of redevelopment in this 
state and the events leading to the demise of former redevelopment agencies, and we 
need not repeat that detailed explanation here. (California Redevelopment Assn. v. 
Matosantos (2011) 53 Cal.4th 231, 242-252.) It suffices to say that in 2011, the 
Legislature passed Assembly Bill No. 1X 26, which dissolved all redevelopment agencies 
in California and transferred their assets to successor agencies. (Health & Saf. Code, 
§§ 34172, subd. (a)(1) & (b), 34173, subd. (a); Assem. Bill No. 1X 26, § 7.) Among 
other things, successor agencies were required to expeditiously wind down the affairs of 
and dispose of all assets and properties of the former redevelopment agency, and transfer 
proceeds from asset sales to the county auditor-controller for distribution to the taxing 
entities. (Health & Saf. Code, §§ 34177, subds. (d), (e), (g), (h), 34181, subd. (a), 
34188.) 
In 2012, the Legislature passed Assembly Bill No. 1484, which required successor 
agencies to prepare a long-range property management plan addressing the disposition 
and use of the real properties of the former redevelopment agency; the plan was required 

2 Further undesignated statutory references are to the Code of Civil Procedure. 
3 
to be submitted for approval to the “oversight board” and the Department of Finance.3 
(Health & Saf. Code, §§ 34191.3, 34191.5.) The law as amended required the liquidation 
and sale of all non-housing assets and properties of the dissolved redevelopment agency 
unless the property fell within one of three exceptions identified in the long-range 
property management plan: (1) properties retained for governmental use; (2) properties 
retained to fulfill an enforceable obligation; and (3) properties retained for future 
development. (Id., § 34191.5, subd. (c)(2).) For properties temporarily retained by the 
city or successor agency for future development, the Legislature required the city or 
successor agency to enter into a compensation agreement with the affected taxing entities 
to provide the taxing entities with payments in proportion to their shares of the base 
property tax for the value of the retained property. (Id., §§ 34180, subd. (f), 34191.5, 
subd. (c)(2)(A)(iii).) 
The Long Range Plan and The Seligman Parcels 
The City of San Diego Redevelopment Agency was dissolved in 2012 as a result 
of the enactment of the Dissolution Law; the City was designated as the successor 
agency. In 2015, the City finalized, and the Department of Finance and oversight board 
approved, the City’s long-range property management plan (Long Range Plan). With 
respect to future development properties, the Long Range Plan provided that the City 
would execute a compensation agreement with the affected taxing entities in exchange 
for the transfer of each future development property to the City in accordance with the 
Long Range Plan. The Long Range Plan further provided that the City reserved the right 
to transfer ownership of any future development property back to the successor agency 
for prompt liquidation in the event the City was unable to execute a compensation 
agreement with the affected taxing entities. 

3 An oversight board has supervisory power over successor agencies. (Health & 
Saf. Code, §§ 34171, subd. (f), 34179.) 
4 
The Long Range Plan identified 22 properties to be retained for future 
development. According to a 2019 memorandum authored by the city attorney, in mid-
2016 the City was unable to negotiate a “master” compensation agreement with the 
affected taxing entities for the 22 future development properties. The City subsequently 
recategorized 10 of the future development properties to liquidation sites and sold them, 
and it entered into compensation agreements for three others. 
In November 2018, Seligman acquired a ground leasehold interest in several 
parcels contained within one of the future development properties that had been retained 
by the City and was lacking a compensation agreement (Seligman Parcels). In 2021, 
Seligman unsuccessfully attempted to purchase the City’s leased fee interest in the 
Seligman Parcels. 
Seligman’s Petition for Writ of Mandate 
In March 2022, Seligman filed a petition for writ of mandate alleging that the City 
violated the Dissolution Law by retaining at least 26 properties it was legally required to 
sell (which they referred to as the Wrongfully Retained Properties), including the 
Seligman Parcels, and had failed to meaningfully attempt to develop or sell the sites or 
enter into compensation agreements. Seligman requested that the trial court issue a writ 
directing the City to recategorize the subject properties from “future development” to 
“liquidation/sale,” to transfer title to the subject properties to the successor agency, and 
for the successor agency to expeditiously sell the subject properties and disburse the net 
sale proceeds to the affected taxing entities. Seligman further requested that the court 
retain continuing jurisdiction until the subject properties had been sold and the proceeds 
transferred, and for “such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.” 
Seligman attached the Long Range Plan to the petition. 
The parties filed briefs in advance of the hearing. Seligman’s brief requested 
relief similar to that sought in the petition, and further proposed an extensive and specific 
process for the sale of the subject properties. In opposition, the City argued in part that it 
5 
did not have a duty to sell any property, the Dissolution Law did not establish a time 
frame for entering into compensation agreements, Seligman’s requested relief would 
violate the Dissolution Law and the Long Range Plan, and forcing it to sell the subject 
properties would amount to a windfall for Seligman and a substantial loss for everyone 
else. 
Trial Court Ruling 
The trial court issued a tentative ruling rejecting the City’s affirmative defenses 
and agreeing in part with Seligman. The court agreed with the City that the Dissolution 
Law did not mandate any particular time frame within which a compensation agreement 
must be reached for a future development property, but it observed that interpreting the 
Dissolution Law to impose no deadline for negotiating compensation agreements would 
render the language directing a city to negotiate such agreements effectively meaningless. 
The court noted there was no evidence that the City had taken any action to negotiate a 
compensation agreement (after the failure to enter into a master compensation agreement 
in mid-2016) or liquidate any of the subject properties in the eight years after the 
approval of the Long Range Plan, and thus there was no indication that the City had 
“complied with its obligation to exercise its discretion to either pursue Compensation 
Agreements or transfer specific Future Development properties for liquidation.” 
The trial court concluded that Seligman had not demonstrated entitlement to any 
of the specific relief prayed for in the petition for writ of mandate. However, based on 
the petition’s request for “such other and further relief as the Court deems just and 
proper,” the court determined that the City had a mandatory duty to begin exercising in 
good faith its discretion to either actively pursue compensation agreements or transfer 
ownership of the subject properties for which compensation agreements could not be 
6 
reached.4 The court’s tentative ruling declined Seligman’s request that it retain 
jurisdiction over the matter until compensation agreements were reached or the subject 
properties were sold. 
On October 2, 2023, after the hearing, the trial court issued its final ruling. The 
court noted Seligman’s argument, made at the hearing, that the relief outlined in the 
tentative ruling was insufficient, and that the court should either: (1) require the City to 
transfer the subject properties to the successor agency because the “ ‘reasonable time’ ” 
for negotiating compensation agreements had passed; (2) provide a deadline for the City 
to reach compensation agreements for the subject properties, or; (3) retain jurisdiction 
until the City had completed negotiation of all compensation agreements or had 
transferred the properties for which compensation agreements could not be reached to the 
successor agency for liquidation. The court declined to adopt Seligman’s 
recommendations, and instead modified its tentative ruling to order the City to make and 
file a return within 60 days after issuance of the writ, and each 60 days thereafter, setting 
forth what it had done to comply therewith. The court retained jurisdiction over the 
matter until it received and granted a request to discharge the writ. 
The trial court incorporated its ruling into the judgment and subsequently issued 
the writ. No party filed an appeal. 
Seligman’s Motion for Attorney Fees 
Seligman filed a postjudgment motion for attorney fees. They claimed 
$322,798.50 in fees for 442.2 attorney hours and 71.8 paralegal hours, plus anticipated 
time for preparation of the reply brief and attending the hearing, pursuant to section 

4 The trial court excepted certain sites that were held by the successor agency, not 
the City. 
7 
1021.5,5 the common fund doctrine, and the substantial benefit theory. The motion noted 
that Seligman had been represented throughout the litigation by two attorneys, “one of 
whom took ‘senior counsel’ or ‘of counsel’ status and has recently retired from the 
practice of law.” Declarations filed in support of the motion by Seligman’s two 
attorneys, William Ihrke and Jeffrey Oderman, clarified that Oderman had gone on 
inactive status with the California Bar Association on February 1, 2023. Oderman 
attached as an exhibit to his declaration det

IN THE APPELLATE COURT 

OF ILLINOIS 

FOURTH DISTRICT 

MICHELMANN STEEL CONSTRUCTION 
COMPANY, an Illinois Corporation, 
 Plaintiff-Appellee and Cross-Appellant, 
 v. 
LINK MEDIA MIDWEST, LLC, a Delaware Limited 
Liability Company, 
 Defendant-Appellant and Cross-Appellee.

 JUSTICE CAVANAGH delivered the judgment of the court. 
 Justices DeArmond and Grischow concurred in the judgment. 

ORDER 

¶ 1 Held: (1) Unless the lease agreement provides the tenant a reasonable time after 
termination of the lease for removal of trade fixtures and other personal property 
of the tenant, the tenant must remove such personal property while the tenant is in 
possession of the premises in the character of a tenant during the original lease 
term, a renewed lease, or a successive lease, and if the tenant fails to do so, the 
property becomes the landlord’s property. 

(2) Absent a demonstration by citation to relevant authorities that the replacement 
value of the property, as opposed to its fair market value, is a valid measure of 
damages for conversion, plaintiff failed to prove the damages resulting from the 
conversion and, consequently, was entitled to only nominal damages for the 
conversion. 

(3) Because plaintiff makes no reasoned argument, supported by relevant 
authorities, regarding its claim of tortious interference with business relationships, 
plaintiff has forfeited the issue of whether the circuit court erred by finding 
against plaintiff on that claim. 

(4) As plaintiff elected to treat defendant as a holdover tenant, there was a new 
lease for the original one-year term, subject, however, to the other provisions in 
the original lease agreement, including the provision that the lease would continue

¶ 2 In the Adams County circuit court, plaintiff, Michelmann Steel Corporation 
(Michelmann), sued defendant, Link Media Midwest, LLC (Link Media), for conversion, 
tortious interference with business relationships, and breach of contract—counts I, II, and III of 
the complaint, respectively. At the conclusion of a bench trial, in which only documentary 
evidence was presented, the court found in Michelmann’s favor on count III but found in Link 
Media’s favor on the remaining two counts. Link Media appeals, and Michelmann cross-appeals. 
¶ 3 In our de novo review, we agree with the circuit court’s judgment, except for the 
finding against Michelmann on count I. Michelmann proved conversion. Nevertheless, because 
Michelmann failed to prove the fair market value of the converted property, it is entitled to only 
nominal damages on count I. 
¶ 4 Therefore, we affirm the circuit court’s judgment in part, reverse it in part, and 
remand this case with directions. We reverse the judgment insomuch as the court found in favor 
of Link Media and against Michelmann on count I. We remand this case with directions to enter 
judgment in favor of Michelmann and against Link Media on count I and to award nominal 
damages to Michelmann for conversion. Otherwise, we affirm the judgment. 
¶ 5 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 6 A. The Complaint and the Answer 
¶ 7 In count I of its complaint, Michelmann alleged that on April 19, 2019, Link 
Media, the assignee of Michelmann’s previous lessee, Outdoor Graphics, Inc. (Outdoor 
Graphics), “dismantled and removed” the “Billboard Structures” on the premises—a lot on 24th 
Street in Quincy, Illinois (the lot)—and thereby converted the “Billboard Structures.” In its 
answer to count I, Link Media admitted that Outdoor Graphics had assigned its interest in the 
- 3 - 
lease to Link Media and that on April 19, 2019, Link Media had the “Billboard Structures” 
removed from the lot. Link Media denied, however, that the “Billboard Structures” belonged to 
Michelmann and, hence, that the removal of them was a conversion. 
¶ 8 Count II of the complaint was an action against Link Media for tortious 
interference with prospective business relationships. In that count, Michelmann alleged it had 
“possessed a reasonable expectation of entering valid business relationships in regards to the 
Billboard Structures” and that, “[b]y willfully and maliciously removing the Billboard Structures 
from Michelmann’s property,” Link Media had “intentionally acted in such a manner so as to 
disrupt, destroy[,] and interfere with” Michelmann’s “prospective business opportunities” to rent 
the “Billboard Structures” to “prospective customers.” Because Link Media disputed 
Michelmann’s ownership of the “Billboard Structures,” Link Media disputed it had committed 
this tort as well. 
¶ 9 The remaining count of Michelmann’s complaint, count III, was an action against 
Link Media for breach of contract in that Link Media allegedly had breached the lease agreement 
by failing to pay rent to Michelmann in return for its permission to engage in billboard 
advertising on the lot. In its answer to count III, Link Media admitted that, “at one point in time, 
Link Media’s predecessors in interest agreed to pay Michelmann [$400] per year for the lease of 
land beginning on May 1, 1987[,] with annual increases in rent in the amount of [10%]”, but 
Link Media denied it had defaulted on that obligation to pay rent. 
¶ 10 B. Evidence at the Bench Trial 
¶ 11 1. Lease Agreements 
¶ 12 There was a bench trial, and the parties tried the case solely on written 
submissions. The documentary evidence was essentially as follows, beginning with a series of 
- 4 - 
lease agreements between Michelmann and various lessees. 
¶ 13 On May 8, 1956, for $50 a year, Michelmann granted to Quincy Outdoor 
Advertising Co. (Quincy Outdoor) “sole and exclusive permission” to “build and maintain two 
Standard Poster Panels to be used for advertising” on the lot. This lease agreement was to “hold 
good” until Michelmann sold the lot or erected a permanent building on it, “in which event thirty 
days[’] notice, in writing,” was to be given to Quincy Outdoor. However, Quincy Outdoor might 
terminate the lease “at any time” by giving Michelmann 30 days’ written notice. Michelmann 
agreed that, upon the lease’s being “terminated at any time,” it would “refund all monies 
advanced, pro rata, for the unexpired part of the current year” and would allow “the removal of 
all boards, etc., the property of” Quincy Outdoor. 
¶ 14 In a request for admission pursuant to Illinois Supreme Court Rule 216 (eff. July 
1, 2014), Michelmann requested that Link Media admit that Link Media did “not know when the 
billboard structures, formerly located on the Premises and removed by Link [Media] in 2019, 
were erected.” Link Media answered, “Deny. The original billboard would have been 
constructed after May 8, 1956[,] and before July 8, 1968, according to the leases.” 
¶ 15 The next lease in the record was to Busby Outdoor, Inc. (Busby). On July 8, 1968, 
Michelmann and Busby agreed that, for $80 a year, Michelmann would lease to Busby “space 
for two (2) standard poster panels” on the lot. This lease was to be for an original term of one 
year, but there was an automatic renewal provision. “After the original term hereof,” the lease 
agreement provided, 
“this lease shall continue in force from year to year for a period of five (5)

additional year thereafter, upon written notice of termination to [Michelmann] by

additional year.” 
As long as Busby was its tenant, Michelmann “guarantee[d] to [Busby] free access to and use of 
any part of any structure on said premises as may be necessary for [Busby] to hang scaffolds, or 
construct, post, paint, illuminate, repair or remove its advertisements and structures.” The parties 
further agreed that “[a]ll structures, materials[,] and equipment placed upon said premises by 
[Busby] shall always remain [Busby’s] personal property and may be removed by [Busby] at any

¶ 16 On March 31, 1969, Busby again leased from Michelmann “space for two (2)

¶ 17 On May 8, 1970, Michelmann leased to Mid-States Communications (Quincy),

¶ 18 On May 8, 1971, Michelmann again leased to Mid-States “space for two (2)

¶ 19 On May 6, 1981, Michelmann leased to Outdoor Graphics, for an original term of

¶ 20 On May 1, 1987, Michelmann again leased to Outdoor Graphics, “for an original

agreement is the one that Michelmann sued Link Media for breaching as an assignee of Outdoor

“After the original term hereof this lease shall continue in force from year to year
